subject: zoology
question_text: Describe the respiratory system of cockroach with the help of neat and labelled diagrams.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack zoology section (book p.23-24, LAQ 8). Zoology holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no zoology board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. APPEARANCES: the book prints [AP M-16,18] and [TS M-15,19]. ONE POINT DIFFERS BETWEEN SOURCES and this card follows the source book: which spiracles open during inspiration. The book says the two thoracic pairs stay open and the eight abdominal pairs stay closed during inspiration, and the reverse during expiration; several other texts print the first four pairs open during inspiration and the last six during expiration. A teacher must settle this before the card is taught. The book's question line ends with a question mark; the wording is kept verbatim and only the punctuation is cleaned. The book prints TWO diagrams for it (the whole-body tracheal plan and a tracheole inset pair); this card draws one combined figure that carries both. FIGURE SCOPE: the book prints a whole-body tracheal plan plus two tracheole insets; this card draws only the whole-body plan a student can reproduce — ten pairs of spiracles, the longitudinal trunks, the commissural tracheae and one trachea branching into tracheoles.

steps.label: Parts of the system
lines: The cockroach breathes through a tracheal
system. Air tubes carry the air straight to
the tissues, so the blood does not carry it.
The tracheal system has three parts —
stigmata (spiracles), tracheae and
tracheoles.
Breathing itself has two events, inspiration
and expiration.
steps.why: Naming the three parts in order from outside to inside gives the answer its plan: air enters at the spiracles, travels in the tracheae and is delivered by the tracheoles.
common_mistakes: Writing that the blood carries oxygen to the tissues. Haemolymph has no respiratory pigment; the tracheoles do that work.
Naming only the tracheae. Spiracles and tracheoles are separate named parts.
steps.memory_tip: Outside to inside: spiracle, trachea, tracheole — big opening, big tube, fine tube.
steps.margin_note: Three parts of the tracheal system plus the two events of breathing. Three short lines.

steps.label: Diagram — tracheal system

elements.caption: Step 1 — body outline and the head
Step 2 — ten pairs of spiracles: 2 thoracic, 8 abdominal
Step 3 — atria and the three longitudinal trunks
Step 4 — cephalic trunks and commissural tracheae
Step 5 — a trachea ending in tracheoles

steps.why: The count and the position of the spiracles are the marked facts, and a drawing shows them faster than a sentence: two pairs on the thorax, eight pairs down the abdomen, joined by the longitudinal trunks.
common_mistakes: Drawing an unequal number of spiracles on the two sides. They are in ten PAIRS, so both sides match.
Putting all ten pairs on the abdomen. The first two pairs are thoracic.
Leaving out the commissural tracheae that join the trunks of the two sides.
steps.memory_tip: Draw the body outline, mark 2 pairs on the thorax and 8 pairs down the abdomen, then run the trunks between them and join the sides across.
steps.margin_note: Label thoracic and abdominal spiracles, the cephalic trunks, the three longitudinal trunks, the atrium and the commissural trachea.

steps.label: Stigmata (spiracles)
lines: Stigmata (spiracles): the outer openings of
the tracheal system. They lie on the pleura.
There are ten pairs. The first two pairs are
thoracic and the remaining eight pairs are
abdominal.
The system is called polypneustic, because
more than three pairs are present, and
holopneustic, because all of them work.
Every spiracle has a valve and is held open
by a chitinous ring called the peritreme.
Hair-like trichomes inside it filter dust
from the incoming air.
steps.why: Two words carry this step's mark, polypneustic and holopneustic, and both are defined by the count itself, so the ten pairs must be stated before the terms are used.
common_mistakes: Writing ten spiracles instead of ten PAIRS, which is twenty openings.
Swapping the two terms. Polypneustic is about the number; holopneustic is about all of them working.
steps.memory_tip: Two plus eight makes ten pairs. Poly = many pairs, holo = all of them open.
steps.margin_note: Ten pairs with the two-plus-eight split, both terms with their meanings, peritreme and trichomes. One mark.

steps.label: Tracheae
lines: Tracheae: each spiracle opens inside into a
small chamber called an atrium.
In the thorax, tracheae from the atria join
to form the dorso-cephalic and the
ventro-cephalic trunks, whose branches
supply the head. Lateral longitudinal trunks
are also present.
From each abdominal atrium three tubes arise.
They open into the dorsal, lateral and
ventral longitudinal trunks.
The trunks of the two sides are joined by
commissural tracheae, and branches pass from
them to all parts of the body.
The tracheal wall has three layers — an outer
basement membrane, a middle epithelium and
an inner cuticle called intima.
The intima is thickened in a spiral called
taenidia. It stops the tube collapsing when
there is no air in it.
steps.why: The tracheae are described twice over, once as a plan of trunks and once as a wall of three layers, and the taenidia is the detail that explains why an air tube stays open at all.
common_mistakes: Writing that the spiracle opens straight into a trunk. It opens into an atrium first.
Calling the taenidia a layer. It is a spiral thickening OF the intima, the innermost layer.
Giving two wall layers. Three are expected: basement membrane, epithelium and intima.
steps.memory_tip: Three longitudinal trunks along the body, three wall layers across it, and one spiral, the taenidia, holding the tube open.
steps.margin_note: Atria, the cephalic trunks, the three longitudinal trunks, commissural tracheae, then the three wall layers and taenidia. Two marks.

steps.label: Tracheoles
lines: Tracheoles: each trachea ends in a
tracheoblast cell, which holds many fine
tubules called tracheoles inside it.
Tracheoles have no intima and no taenidia.
Their inner surface is lined by a protein
called trachein.
They are filled with tracheolar fluid, and
they deliver the air to the tissues.
steps.why: The tracheoles are where gas exchange actually happens, and their two differences from a trachea, no taenidia and a fluid filling, are exactly what a fine exchange surface needs.
common_mistakes: Writing that tracheoles have taenidia. Both intima and taenidia are absent in tracheoles.
Calling the tracheole lining chitin. It is a protein called trachein.
steps.memory_tip: Trachea has taenidia; tracheole has trachein and fluid. Same start, opposite lining.
steps.margin_note: Tracheoblast cell, no intima or taenidia, trachein, tracheolar fluid. Four facts for one mark.

steps.label: Mechanism of breathing

lines.text: Inspiration is passive, expiration is active

lines: The dorsoventral and the ventral longitudinal
muscles carry out both events.
Inspiration: these muscles relax, the body
volume increases and air is drawn into the
tracheae. The thoracic spiracles stay open
and the abdominal spiracles stay closed.
Inspiration uses no energy, so it is passive.
Expiration: the thoracic spiracles close, the
abdominal spiracles open and the air is
pushed out. Expiration uses energy, so it is
active.
The spiracles open and close according to the
carbon dioxide level in the haemolymph and
the oxygen level in the tracheae.
steps.why: This step names which muscles move, which spiracles are open at each event, and which event costs energy, so the two events can be told apart in a single line each.
common_mistakes: Writing that inspiration is active. Inspiration is passive; expiration is the active one.
Saying the muscles contract during inspiration. They RELAX, so the body volume increases.
steps.memory_tip: In through the thorax, out through the abdomen. Passive in, active out.
steps.margin_note: Two named muscle sets, then one line each for inspiration and expiration with which spiracles are open. One mark.

insider_note: The mark most often lost here is 'ten pairs' written as 'ten', and the second is the passive-active pair — write inspiration passive and expiration active in those exact words, because that is the line the examiner scans for.
